quests.d: Powers of two, data units, and doing big multiplications in your head
quests.goal: Your win today: you can say '2 to the 30 is about a billion, so a gigabyte', multiply '300 million users times 1 KB' in your head (300 GB), and you never write a number on the whiteboard without its unit.
quests.bookSections: Chapter 2 intro (Jeff Dean's definition of back-of-the-envelope estimation), 'Power of two' (Table 2-1), and the 'Tips' section items on rounding/approximation and labeling units

stages.title: Climb the byte ladder
stages.sub: Five rungs that cover every estimate you'll ever do
stages.teaches: Opening idea (book, quoting Jeff Dean, Google Senior Fellow): back-of-the-envelope calculations are estimates you build from thought experiments plus common performance numbers, to get a feel for which designs will meet your requirements. Interviewers use them to see whether you can reason about scale; precision is not the point. Data volume can get huge but the arithmetic is simple once you know the units. A byte is 8 bits. One ASCII character (plain English letter, digit, punctuation) takes 1 byte. Table 2-1: 2^10 ≈ 1 thousand = 1 KB (kilobyte); 2^20 ≈ 1 million = 1 MB (megabyte); 2^30 ≈ 1 billion = 1 GB (gigabyte); 2^40 ≈ 1 trillion = 1 TB (terabyte); 2^50 ≈ 1 quadrillion = 1 PB (petabyte). Pattern: every +10 in the exponent = ×~1000 = next unit = 3 more zeros.
stages.interaction: A vertical ladder with five empty rungs labeled 2^10, 2^20, 2^30, 2^40, 2^50 (bottom to top). Below it, two shuffled trays of chips: word chips (thousand, million, billion, trillion, quadrillion) and unit chips (KB, MB, GB, TB, PB). Learner taps a chip, then taps a rung to place it (tap-to-place, works on mobile). A rung lights up green and shows '≈ 10^3', '≈ 10^6'… when both its chips are right; wrong placements shake and bounce the chip back (no heart cost here, practice). When all 10 chips are placed, an animated '×1000' arrow appears between each rung and a byte counter at the top rolls from 1 KB up to 1 PB. A small side card shows 'A = 1 byte (ASCII), 1 byte = 8 bits'.
stages.check: Q.quiz: '2^30 bytes is about…' options: '1 billion bytes, which is 1 GB' (correct) / '1 million bytes, which is 1 MB' / '1 trillion bytes, which is 1 TB'. Good: 'Every +10 on the exponent is ×1000 and one unit up: 10→KB, 20→MB, 30→GB.'

stages.title: The 2.4% white lie
stages.sub: Why 1024 ≈ 1000 is fine, and where it starts to drift
stages.teaches: 2^10 is really 1,024, not 1,000, so the ladder is an approximation: the error is 2.4% at KB, 4.9% at MB, 7.4% at GB, 10.0% at TB, 12.6% at PB. For an estimate that's off by at most ~13%, which is well inside 'right order of magnitude'. Real-world wrinkle: the IEC binary units KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB (kibibyte etc.) mean exact powers of two; KB/MB/GB officially mean powers of ten. Disk makers sell decimal TB, operating systems often report binary units, so a '1 TB' drive shows up as about 931 'GB' (really GiB). In an interview, say 'I'll treat 2^10 as 1,000' and move on.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch. First the learner predicts: 'How far off is 2^40 from 10^12 (one trillion)?' options 0.1% / 2.4% / 10% / 50%. Then a 'drift meter': a horizontal slider with stops at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. At each stop two bars render side by side: exact 2^n (e.g. 1,099,511,627,776) vs the round 10^(3k) (1,000,000,000,000), and a gauge shows the gap % (2.4, 4.9, 7.4, 10.0, 12.6). A gauge band from 0–25% is shaded green and labeled 'fine for napkin math'. Then a mini card: a '1 TB' drive icon; learner taps 'What does the OS show?' and it animates 1,000,000,000,000 ÷ 1024³ = 931 GiB.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: 10%). Then Q.quiz: 'Your interviewer says 2^40 is 1.1 trillion, not 1 trillion. Best reply?' options: 'True, about 10% off; fine at this level of estimate' (correct) / 'Then I need to redo every number exactly' / 'No, 2^40 is exactly one trillion bytes'.

stages.title: Count the zeros
stages.sub: Big multiplications without a calculator
stages.teaches: The trick: rewrite each number as (small number) × 10^k, multiply the small numbers, add the exponents, then map the exponent back to a unit (3→K, 6→M, 9→G, 12→T, 15→P). Example: 300 million users × 1 KB = 3×10^8 × 10^3 bytes = 3×10^11 bytes = 300 GB. 150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB = 1.5×10^8 × 2 × 0.1 × 10^6 = 3×10^13 bytes = 30 TB (the exact Twitter media number from Quest 2.4). Percentages are just ×0.1, ×0.5 etc.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check, 4 cards in sequence. Each card shows a problem and a 'zero tally' helper: each factor appears as a chip with its mantissa and exponent (e.g. '3 × 10^8', '1 × 10^3 B'); the learner can tap a chip to see its exponent highlighted. Answer box = number field + unit dropdown (B, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB). Problems: (1) 300 million users × 1 KB profile → 300 GB; (2) 2 billion photos × 500 KB → 1 PB (1,000 TB accepted); (3) 10 million users × 2 KB → 20 GB; (4) 150 million × 2 tweets × 10% × 1 MB → 30 TB. Grading accepts any value/unit pair equivalent within ±10% (so '0.3 TB' passes for 300 GB). On a wrong answer it animates the worked line: mantissas multiply on the left, exponents add on the right, then the exponent snaps to its unit on the ladder from stage 1.
stages.check: Each card awards XP on first try; after the 4 cards, Q.quiz: '50 million users × 200 bytes of text each is about…' options '10 GB' (correct) / '10 TB' / '10 MB'.

stages.title: Round like a pro
stages.sub: The book's tips: approximate, and label every unit
stages.teaches: Book tip 1, rounding and approximation: doing 99987 / 9.1 by hand wastes interview time; round to 100,000 / 10 = 10,000. Precision is not expected. Book tip 2, label your units: writing '5' on the board is ambiguous; is it 5 KB or 5 MB? You will confuse yourself. Write 5 MB. Bonus handy constant (not in the book, but standard): a day has 86,400 seconds ≈ 10^5, so 1 million events per day ≈ 10 per second (exactly 11.6), and 1 billion per day ≈ 10,000 per second (exactly 11,574).
stages.interaction: Two mini-games. (A) Rounding sprint: 5 ugly expressions appear one at a time (99,987 / 9.1; 86,400 × 3; 1,000,000 / 86,400; 47 × 2,100; 3.65 × 300). For each, the learner first picks the best rounded form from 3 options (e.g. '100,000 / 10', '99,990 / 9', '99,987 / 9'), then the answer appears with exact vs rounded side by side and the % gap. A small stopwatch shows how long they took (no penalty; it just shows that rounding is fast). (B) Spot the unit bug: a whiteboard image with 5 lines of an estimate, e.g. 'DAU = 150 million', 'Tweet size = 1', 'Media/day = 30 TB', 'QPS ≈ 3500', 'Storage/5 yrs = 55'. Learner taps every line missing a unit (correct: 'Tweet size = 1' and 'Storage/5 yrs = 55'; QPS is fine because the unit is in its name). Tapped lines get a red underline and a tooltip suggesting the fix ('1 MB', '55 PB').
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Why does the book say to label units?' options: 'So you don't mix up 5 KB and 5 MB halfway through the math' (correct) / 'Interviewers grade you on SI notation style' / 'Units make the numbers more precise'.

stages.title: Boss: The Unit Gremlin
stages.sub: Grade the whiteboard before the interviewer does
stages.teaches: Applies stages 1–4: unit ladder, zero counting, rounding, labeling. The common bugs are off-by-1000 (one rung slipped), missing units, and fake precision.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with shared choices: '✅ Looks right', '🔢 Off by about 1000×', '📏 Unit missing', '🎯 Fake precision, round it'. Scenarios (each a whiteboard line): (1) '1 million users × 1 KB = 1 GB' → Looks right; (2) '2^40 bytes ≈ 1 PB' → Off by 1000× (it's 1 TB); (3) 'Write QPS = 3,472.2222' → Fake precision (say ~3,500); (4) 'Daily media storage: 30' → Unit missing (30 TB); (5) '5 million users × 2 MB = 10 GB' → Off by 1000× (it's 10 TB); (6) '1 billion ASCII characters ≈ 1 GB' → Looks right (1 byte each); (7) 'Peak QPS = 6,944.44 per second' → Fake precision. Each 'why' shows the corrected line.
stages.check: Boss HP bar; a wrong pick costs a heart in a first run (engine default).

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: The 30-second unit talk
stages.teaches: Recall of the whole quest in the learner's own words.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'The interviewer says: you have 300 million users and each profile is about 1 KB. How much storage, and how did you get there so fast?' Model answer: '300 million is 3 × 10^8, 1 KB is 10^3 bytes, add the exponents: 3 × 10^11 bytes, which is 300 GB. I'm treating 2^10 as 1,000; that's about 2.4% off per step, around 10% by terabytes, which is fine for an estimate. I'll write it as 300 GB with the unit, and round as I go, because precision isn't the point.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Converted to powers of ten and added exponents', 'Got 300 GB (with the unit)', 'Said 2^10 ≈ 1,000 and that the error is small', 'Mentioned rounding / precision not expected'.

caveats: 2^10 = 1,024, not 1,000: the ladder drifts by 2.4% per rung (about 10% at TB, 12.6% at PB). Fine for estimates, wrong for billing or capacity contracts.
Strictly, KB/MB/GB are decimal (10^3, 10^6, 10^9) and KiB/MiB/GiB are binary (2^10…). The book blurs them, as most engineers do in conversation.
'1 ASCII character = 1 byte' holds for English text; real text is UTF-8, where non-Latin characters take 2–4 bytes and emoji take 4.
The 86,400 ≈ 10^5 shortcut is not in the book; it underestimates rates by about 14%, which is why the book's Twitter example says ~3,500 QPS while the shortcut gives ~3,000.

quests.d: Latency numbers every programmer should know, and the five lessons in them
quests.winTitle: You can feel a nanosecond now
quests.goal: Your win today: you can rank memory, disk, data-center and cross-ocean costs from memory, quote the rough numbers (100 ns, 10 ms, 0.5 ms, 150 ms), and use them to justify a cache, batching, or compression.
quests.bookSections: 'Latency numbers every programmer should know' (Table 2-2, Figure 2-1 visualization, and the five conclusions)

stages.title: Order the universe
stages.sub: Sort 13 operations from fastest to slowest
stages.teaches: Units: ns = nanosecond = 10^-9 s; µs = microsecond = 10^-6 s = 1,000 ns; ms = millisecond = 10^-3 s = 1,000 µs. Table 2-2 (Jeff Dean's numbers, roughly 2010-era hardware): L1 cache reference 0.5 ns; branch mispredict 5 ns; L2 cache reference 7 ns; mutex lock/unlock 100 ns; main memory reference 100 ns; compress 1 KB with Zippy (Google's fast compressor, open-sourced as Snappy) 10 µs; send 2 KB over a 1 Gbps network 20 µs; read 1 MB sequentially from memory 250 µs; round trip within the same data center 500 µs; disk seek 10 ms; read 1 MB sequentially from the network 10 ms; read 1 MB sequentially from disk 30 ms; send a packet California → Netherlands → California 150 ms.
stages.interaction: Sort/order mechanic: 13 operation cards shuffled in a column (each card has an icon: CPU chip, RAM stick, spinning disk, network, globe). Learner taps cards in order from fastest to slowest; each tapped card slides into a numbered 'ladder' on the right. Ties (mutex = main memory = 100 ns; disk seek = 1 MB from network = 10 ms) accept either order. After all are placed, the cards reveal their times and re-arrange onto a horizontal log-scale bar chart (each gridline = ×10, from 0.1 ns to 1 s), with misplaced cards outlined in amber and an arrow showing where they belong. Score shows 'X of 13 in the right spot' (counting ties as correct).
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Which is slower: one disk seek, or a round trip to another server in the same data center?' options: 'The disk seek: 10 ms vs 0.5 ms, about 20× slower' (correct) / 'The data-center round trip, because networks are slow' / 'They take about the same time'.

stages.title: If an L1 hit took one second
stages.sub: Stretch time until your gut understands it
stages.teaches: Humans can't feel nanoseconds, so stretch everything by the same factor (×2 billion makes 0.5 ns = 1 s). Then: main memory 100 ns ≈ 3.3 minutes; compress 1 KB ≈ 5.6 hours; data-center round trip 500 µs ≈ 11.6 days; disk seek 10 ms ≈ 7.6 months; read 1 MB from disk 30 ms ≈ 1.9 years; California→Netherlands→California 150 ms ≈ 9.5 years. The gaps are what matter: memory vs disk seek is 100,000×; in-DC vs cross-ocean is 300×. (This human-scale framing is a popular teaching device, not from the book.)
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch. Prompt: 'If an L1 cache hit took 1 second, a disk seek would take about…' options: 'a minute' / 'a day' / 'about 8 months' / 'a century'. After the pick, a vertical timeline zooms out: a clock icon at 1 s, then a 'go make coffee' marker at 3.3 min (memory), a 'sleep on it' marker at 5.6 h (compress), a calendar at 11.6 days (DC round trip), a season change at 7.6 months (disk seek), and finally a '9.5 years' marker (cross-ocean) as the camera keeps zooming out. A toggle switches between 'real time' and 'human time' labels for every operation in the table.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: about 8 months). Then Q.quiz: 'Roughly how many main-memory reads fit in one disk seek?' options: '100,000' (correct: 10 ms ÷ 100 ns) / '100' / '10 million'.

stages.title: Five lessons, four duels
stages.sub: The book's conclusions, proven with a stopwatch
stages.teaches: The book's conclusions from the table: (1) memory is fast but disk is slow; (2) avoid disk seeks if possible; (3) simple compression algorithms are fast; (4) compress data before sending it over the internet if possible; (5) data centers are usually in different regions, and sending data between them takes time. What this means in design: keep hot data in memory (caches), read sequentially rather than seeking randomly, batch calls that cross regions, and shrink bytes before they cross slow, metered links.
stages.interaction: Four head-to-head duels. Each shows two request paths built from operation blocks from the table; the learner predicts which finishes first and roughly by how much (×2 / ×10 / ×100+), then taps 'Race' and two progress bars animate on a time axis (scaled), with totals. Duel 1: read a 1 MB profile blob from memory (250 µs) vs disk seek + 1 MB disk read (10 ms + 30 ms = 40 ms) → memory wins by ~160×. Duel 2: 100 random disk seeks for 100 small records (100 × 10 ms = 1 s) vs one sequential 1 MB read holding all of them (30 ms) → sequential ~33× faster. Duel 3: 5 sequential calls to a service in another region (5 × 150 ms = 750 ms) vs 1 batched call (150 ms) vs 5 calls to a service in the same DC (5 × 0.5 ms = 2.5 ms). Duel 4: compress a 100 KB response (100 × 10 µs = 1 ms) before a cross-ocean trip vs sending it raw; the bar shows the 1 ms compression as a sliver next to the 150 ms round trip, with a note that the real win is fewer bytes on a slow, metered link. After each duel, the matching book conclusion card flips over.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Your API calls a user service in another continent 8 times, one after another, per page load. What's the cheapest big win?' options: 'Batch the calls or keep a copy of the data in the same region' (correct) / 'Buy faster CPUs for the API servers' / 'Switch from L2 to L1 cache on the API boxes'.

stages.title: Old numbers, new hardware
stages.sub: What has changed since 2010, and what never will
stages.teaches: The table is from around 2010. CPU caches and RAM latency have barely moved since. Disks changed most: SSDs (solid-state drives) have no moving head, so a random read costs tens of microseconds instead of a 10 ms seek; sequential reads on NVMe SSDs run at gigabytes per second. Networks went from 1 Gbps to 10–100 Gbps inside data centers. What can't improve is the speed of light: light in fiber travels at about 200,000 km/s, so California↔Netherlands (about 9,000 km by great circle, longer by cable) has a physical round-trip floor of ~90 ms; real routes give ~140–150 ms. Colin Scott's interactive page (book reference [3]) shows the numbers by year (later years are extrapolated, not measured). Interview takeaway: quote the book numbers, then add 'SSDs shrink the disk gap, but cross-region latency is physics'.
stages.interaction: A 'then vs now' toggle over the log-scale chart from stage 1: flipping to 'today (approx.)' slides the disk bars far left (spinning-disk seek 10 ms → SSD random read ~0.1 ms or less, 1 MB sequential from SSD ~1 ms or less) and the network bars a bit left, while memory, in-DC round trip and the California↔Netherlands bar barely move. A 'speed of light' button draws a fiber line on a mini world map between California and the Netherlands and computes 9,000 km ÷ 200,000 km/s = 45 ms one way → 90 ms round-trip floor. Label clearly: 'today values are rough ranges, not a benchmark'.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Which number in the table will never get much better with new hardware?' options: 'The cross-ocean round trip; it's bounded by the speed of light' (correct) / 'Disk seek time' / 'Network bandwidth inside a data center'.

stages.title: Boss: The Slow-Request Hydra
stages.sub: Find the head that's eating the latency
stages.teaches: Applies the table: identify the dominant cost in a request path.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with shared choices: '💾 Disk seeks', '🌍 Cross-region round trips', '📦 Too many bytes on the wire', '✅ Fine: memory / same DC'. Scenarios: (1) 'Each feed request does 200 random reads on a spinning disk' → Disk seeks (200 × 10 ms = 2 s); (2) 'A checkout page in Frankfurt calls a pricing service in Oregon 6 times in a row' → Cross-region (~6 × 150 ms ≈ 0.9 s); (3) 'Session lookups hit an in-memory cache in the same data center' → Fine (~0.5 ms round trip); (4) 'The API ships 8 MB of uncompressed JSON to phones on another continent' → Too many bytes (compress; simple compression is cheap); (5) 'A nightly job loads 1 GB by reading row IDs in random order from disk' → Disk seeks (read sequentially instead); (6) 'Rate-limit counters live in RAM on the same box' → Fine (100 ns memory reads).
stages.check: Boss HP; each answer's 'why' shows the arithmetic from Table 2-2.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: Justify a cache with numbers
stages.teaches: Recall: use the latency numbers to defend a design choice.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'Interviewer: why would you put a cache in front of the database? Use numbers.' Model answer: 'A memory reference is about 100 ns and reading 1 MB from memory about 250 µs, while a disk seek is about 10 ms and reading 1 MB from disk about 30 ms, so memory is roughly 100× faster for bulk reads and 100,000× for random access. A cache in the same data center costs a ~0.5 ms round trip, which is still far cheaper than going to disk. I'd also keep calls inside one region, because a cross-ocean round trip is ~150 ms and that's physics. Caveat: these are 2010-era numbers; SSDs shrink the disk gap, but memory is still much faster.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Quoted memory ~100 ns vs disk seek ~10 ms', 'Mentioned the in-DC round trip (~0.5 ms)', 'Mentioned cross-region ~150 ms', 'Noted SSDs changed the disk numbers'.

caveats: Table 2-2 reflects roughly 2010 hardware. Versions of the list differ slightly (Jeff Dean's slides give mutex lock/unlock as 25 ns and some versions give 20 ms for reading 1 MB from disk); the book uses 100 ns and 30 ms. Treat every number as an order of magnitude.
The 10 ms 'disk seek' is a spinning hard drive. SSD random reads take tens of microseconds, so 'avoid disk seeks' is less dramatic today, but memory is still much faster than any disk.
Colin Scott's interactive chart extrapolates later years from trends; it is not a measured benchmark.
Compression's real win across the internet is fewer bytes on slow or metered links; inside a data center, compressing can cost more CPU time than it saves.
The human-scale 'if L1 were one second' framing is a teaching device, not from the book.

quests.d: Availability percentages, SLAs, and how much downtime each nine allows
quests.goal: Your win today: you can turn '99.9%' into 'about 9 hours of downtime a year, 43 minutes a month', explain what an SLA is, and say why chaining services lowers availability.
quests.bookSections: 'Availability numbers' (high availability definition, SLA, cloud provider SLAs, Table 2-3 nines and downtime)

stages.title: What a nine buys you
stages.sub: From 99% to 99.9999%, on a calendar
stages.teaches: High availability = the ability of a system to stay continuously operational for a desirably long period. It's measured as a percentage of time up: 100% means never down; most services sit between 99% and 100%. An SLA (service level agreement) is an agreement between a service provider and its customer that formally defines the uptime the service will deliver. Amazon, Google and Microsoft set their cloud SLAs at 99.9% or above. Uptime is traditionally counted in nines; more nines = less downtime. Table 2-3: 99% → 14.40 min/day, 1.68 h/week, 7.31 h/month, 3.65 days/year. 99.9% → 1.44 min/day, 10.08 min/week, 43.83 min/month, 8.77 h/year. 99.99% → 8.64 s/day, 1.01 min/week, 4.38 min/month, 52.60 min/year. 99.999% → 864 ms/day, 6.05 s/week, 26.30 s/month, 5.26 min/year. 99.9999% → 86.40 ms/day, 604.80 ms/week, 2.63 s/month, 31.56 s/year.
stages.interaction: Predict first: '99.9% uptime allows how much downtime per year?' options: '8.77 hours' / '3.65 days' / '52 minutes'. Then the Nines Dial: a big rotary selector with 2 to 6 nines. Under it, a year strip of 365 small day-cells; the allowed downtime is drawn as a red block (at 99% it covers ~3.65 day-cells; at 99.9% a sliver of one cell; beyond that a magnifier pops out showing minutes/seconds). Four readouts (per day / week / month / year) count up to the Table 2-3 values each time the dial turns. A side caption updates: '2 nines: a bad weekend', '3 nines: one long evening a year', '5 nines: a coffee break a year'.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: 8.77 hours). Q.quiz: 'A cloud SLA promises 99.99%. About how much downtime is that per month?' options: 'About 4.4 minutes' (correct) / 'About 44 minutes' / 'About 26 seconds'.

stages.title: Do the math yourself
stages.sub: Downtime = (1 − availability) × period
stages.teaches: Formula: allowed downtime = (100% − availability) × period. The book's table uses a 365.25-day year (8,766 hours, 525,960 minutes) and a month of 1/12 of that (~30.44 days, ~43,830 minutes). Shortcut: every extra nine divides downtime by 10 (8.77 h → 52.6 min → 5.26 min → 31.6 s per year). Odd targets like 99.95% sit halfway in log terms: 0.05% × 43,830 min ≈ 21.9 min/month.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check, 4 cards. Each shows availability + period, a formula strip '(1 − A) × period' with the learner filling in the number and choosing a unit (s / min / h / days). Cards: (1) 99.9% per month → 43.8 min; (2) 99.99% per year → 52.6 min; (3) 99.95% per month → 21.9 min; (4) 99.5% per year → 43.8 h (1.83 days accepted). Tolerance ±10% and any equivalent unit. On a miss, show the worked line and a 'divide by 10 per nine' staircase graphic linking it to the table.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Going from 99.9% to 99.99% changes yearly downtime from 8.77 hours to…' options: 'about 52.6 minutes, ten times less' (correct) / 'about 4.4 hours, half as much' / 'about 5.3 minutes, a hundred times less'.

stages.title: Chains and spares
stages.sub: Dependencies multiply; redundancy adds nines
stages.teaches: Beyond the book, but interviewers ask it. Series: if a request needs services A AND B AND C, overall availability = A × B × C. Three services at 99.9% each → 0.999³ ≈ 99.7% (≈ 26 hours down a year, three times worse than any one of them). Parallel: if any one of two independent replicas can serve, availability = 1 − (1 − A)². Two 99% boxes → 1 − 0.01² = 99.99%. So redundancy is how you buy nines; long dependency chains are how you lose them. Big caveat: the parallel formula assumes failures are independent. Replicas in the same rack, same region, or running the same bad deploy fail together, so real gains are smaller.
stages.interaction: A drag-and-wire sandbox. Palette of blocks: 'Server 99%', 'Service 99.9%', 'Service 99.99%'. Learner drops blocks between a 'User' node and a 'Done' node, either in a row (series) or stacked (parallel group). A live readout shows overall availability and downtime/year, recomputed on every change, with the formula shown under the readout. Three challenges unlock in turn (no locks; just suggested order): (1) 'Chain three 99.9% services. What do you get?' → ~99.7%; (2) 'Reach at least 99.99% using only 99% servers' → two in parallel; (3) 'Your API (99.99%) depends on a 99.9% database. Fix it to reach at least 99.95% end to end' → add a parallel database replica. Then a 'correlated failure' toggle puts both replicas in one rack; a lightning bolt hits the rack and both die, and the readout shows a warning that the formula assumed independence.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Your feature calls 4 services, each 99.9% available, one after another. Best estimate of end-to-end availability?' options: 'About 99.6%' (correct) / '99.9%, same as each one' / '99.9999%, because there are four of them'.

stages.title: Read the fine print
stages.sub: SLA vs SLO vs SLI, and what an SLA really promises
stages.teaches: The book defines SLA only; the Google SRE book adds two terms you'll hear in senior conversations. SLI (service level indicator) = a measured number, e.g. 'fraction of requests that succeeded in the last 30 days'. SLO (service level objective) = the internal target for that number, e.g. '99.9% of requests succeed'. SLA = the external contract with consequences if missed; cloud SLAs typically pay service credits (a partial refund), they don't guarantee uptime. Teams set the SLO tighter than the SLA so they notice trouble before it costs money. Error budget = 1 − SLO: at 99.9%, about 43 minutes a month of failure you can 'spend' on risky deploys. Exact provider SLA numbers differ per product and change over time; check the current pages (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure are the book's references).
stages.interaction: Sort-into-buckets: 8 statement cards to drop into SLI / SLO / SLA bins. Examples: 'p99 latency measured over 28 days' → SLI; 'We aim for 99.9% of requests to succeed' → SLO; 'If monthly uptime is below 99.99% you get a 10% credit' → SLA; 'Fraction of health checks that passed' → SLI; 'Internal target: 99.95% availability' → SLO; 'Contract with the customer, with refunds if missed' → SLA; 'Error rate over the last hour' → SLI; 'Alert us when we're burning our monthly budget too fast' → SLO. Then an error-budget meter: a month bar with 43.8 minutes of budget (99.9%); the learner clicks 'deploy' events (each costs a random 2–8 minutes of errors) and watches the budget drain, with a note at zero: 'freeze risky launches until the budget recovers'.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'A cloud provider misses its 99.99% SLA one month. What usually happens?' options: 'Customers can claim service credits, a partial refund' (correct) / 'The provider must pay for all customer losses' / 'Nothing, because the SLA is only an internal goal'.

stages.title: Boss: The Nines Merchant
stages.sub: Right-size the target
stages.teaches: Applies the quest: more nines cost more (redundancy, multi-region, on-call). Pick a target that matches the cost of being down.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with per-scenario choices (the engine supports scenario.choices). (1) 'Product wants 99.999% for an internal monthly reporting dashboard.' choices: 'Overkill: 99.9% or less is fine; 5 nines means about 5 minutes a year and costs a lot' (correct) / 'Right target' / 'Too low, aim for 6 nines'. (2) 'Your service calls 5 dependencies at 99.9% each and you promised customers 99.9%.' choices: 'Can't hold it: chained you're near 99.5%, so add redundancy or remove hard dependencies' (correct) / 'Fine, every dependency meets 99.9%' / 'Fine if you add more servers in a row'. (3) 'Two replicas of a 99% service, same rack, same power supply. Claimed availability: 99.99%.' choices: 'Optimistic: shared rack means correlated failures' (correct) / 'Correct, 1 − 0.01²' / 'Too pessimistic'. (4) 'Engineer: 99.9% means we can be down 8.77 hours a month.' choices: 'Wrong: that's per year; per month it's about 43.8 minutes' (correct) / 'Right' / 'Wrong: it's 8.77 minutes a month'. (5) 'A payments API runs at 99%.' choices: 'Too low: that's 3.65 days of failed payments a year' (correct) / 'Right target' / 'Overkill'.
stages.check: Boss HP; each 'why' links back to Table 2-3 or the series/parallel formulas.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: Talk nines in 30 seconds
stages.teaches: Recall: definitions, the table, the multiplication rule.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'Interviewer: what availability would you target here, and what does it mean in practice?' Model answer: 'I'd target three to four nines. 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, 8.8 hours a year; 99.99% allows about 4.4 minutes a month, 53 minutes a year. Every nine is ten times less downtime and usually a lot more cost. Our availability can't beat the product of our hard dependencies, three 99.9% services in a row give about 99.7%, so I'd add redundancy where it counts and keep the failures independent, for example replicas in different zones. Internally I'd set an SLO a bit tighter than any SLA we sign.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Converted a percentage to downtime (e.g. 99.9% ≈ 43 min/month)', 'Said each nine = 10× less downtime', 'Mentioned that chained dependencies multiply', 'Mentioned redundancy with independent failures (or SLO vs SLA)'.

caveats: Table 2-3 uses a 365.25-day year; with 365 days the yearly numbers shift by about 0.07% (e.g. 8.76 vs 8.77 hours). Irrelevant in an interview.
Series/parallel math, SLO/SLI and error budgets are not in the book chapter; they come from the Google SRE book and are common senior-level follow-ups.
Redundancy math assumes independent failures. Real outages are often correlated (shared region, power, config push, bad deploy), so real availability is lower than the formula says.
A provider SLA is a contract with service credits, not a promise that the service will be up; specific SLA percentages differ by product and change over time.

quests.d: The book's worked example: Twitter's QPS and storage, step by step
quests.goal: Your win today: from five written assumptions you can derive ~3,500 write QPS, ~7,000 peak QPS, 30 TB of media a day and ~55 PB over five years, out loud, in under two minutes.
quests.bookSections: 'Example: Estimate Twitter QPS and storage requirements' (assumptions, QPS, peak QPS, average tweet size, media storage, 5-year storage) and the 'Tips' items on writing down assumptions and commonly asked estimates

stages.title: Pin your assumptions
stages.sub: Write them down before any math
stages.teaches: Book tip: write down your assumptions; they're what you and the interviewer check against later. The book's assumptions (it notes these are not real Twitter numbers): 300 million monthly active users (MAU = distinct users in a month); 50% of users use Twitter daily; users post 2 tweets per day on average; 10% of tweets contain media; data is stored for 5 years. DAU (daily active users) = MAU × daily fraction. In a real interview you propose numbers and ask 'does that sound reasonable?' instead of waiting to be told.
stages.interaction: An interviewer chat bubble gives the prompt: 'Estimate Twitter's QPS and storage requirements.' Below, a deck of 8 assumption cards: the 5 real ones plus 3 distractors ('Twitter is written in Scala', 'There are 2,000 engineers', 'Tweets are sorted by time'). Learner drags/taps the cards they need onto a sticky-note board titled 'Assumptions'. Correct cards stick with a pin; distractors slide off with a one-line reason ('doesn't change QPS or storage'). When all 5 are pinned, the interviewer replies 'Sounds reasonable, go ahead', and the board stays visible (sticky) for stages 2–4.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Why write assumptions on the board first?' options: 'So you and the interviewer can check and adjust the math against them' (correct) / 'Because interviewers grade handwriting' / 'So you can skip asking any questions later'.

stages.title: Crunch the QPS
stages.sub: Users → tweets per day → tweets per second → peak
stages.teaches: QPS = queries per second. DAU = 300 million × 50% = 150 million. Tweets per day = 150 million × 2 = 300 million. Tweet QPS = 300 million ÷ 24 hours ÷ 3,600 seconds = 300,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 3,472 ≈ ~3,500. Peak QPS = 2 × QPS ≈ ~7,000 (the book's simple rule: traffic isn't flat, so plan for a peak; 2× is an assumption, not a law). Shortcut check: 86,400 ≈ 10^5 gives 3,000, the same order of magnitude.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check as a 4-step chain. Each step is a row: formula on the left with the learner's own number from the previous step carried in, an input box + unit, and a check button. Steps: DAU (150 million), tweets/day (300 million), write QPS (accept 3,000–4,000; exact 3,472), peak QPS (accept 6,000–8,000). After step 3, a 'precision' chip pops up: if the learner typed 3,472.22, it suggests 'Say ~3,500: precision isn't expected'. A side mini-tool 'seconds in a day' expands to show 24 × 3,600 = 86,400 ≈ 10^5. When done, a little animated counter shows tweets ticking in at ~3,500 per second with a peak spike to ~7,000.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Why compute peak QPS, not just average?' options: 'Servers must handle the busiest moments, not the average' (correct) / 'Peak QPS is what determines storage' / 'Average QPS is always exactly half of peak'.

stages.title: Weigh the storage
stages.sub: Bytes per tweet → terabytes per day → petabytes
stages.teaches: Average tweet size (book): tweet_id 64 bytes, text 140 bytes, media 1 MB. Book estimates only media, since it dominates: media storage per day = 150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB = 30 million media items × 1 MB = 30 TB per day. 5-year media storage = 30 TB × 365 × 5 ≈ 54,750 TB ≈ 55 PB. Sanity check on text: 300 million tweets × ~204 bytes ≈ 61 GB/day, about 500× smaller than media, which is why it's fine to ignore. Bonus (not in book): 30 TB/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 350 MB/s of incoming media, about 2.8 Gbps.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch, then calculate. Predict: 'Which dominates daily storage: tweet text or media?' (text / media / about equal). Then two growing stacks of disk icons animate side by side as the learner computes: left stack 'text' (inputs: tweets/day 300 million × 204 bytes → ~61 GB), right stack 'media' (150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB → 30 TB). The media stack visibly dwarfs text (the text stack is drawn to scale as a tiny sliver with a magnifier). Next card: '5 years' → learner enters 30 TB × 365 × 5; accept 50–60 PB (or 50,000–60,000 TB). A 'zero tally' helper from Quest 2.1 is available on tap.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: media). Q.quiz: 'The book's 5-year media estimate is about…' options: '55 PB' (correct) / '55 TB' / '5.5 EB'.

stages.title: Turn the knobs
stages.sub: What the interviewer asks next
stages.teaches: Book tip: commonly asked estimates are QPS, peak QPS, storage, cache, number of servers. The results scale linearly with each assumption: double DAU → double everything; double media share → double media storage; peak factor changes QPS but not storage; retention changes total storage but not daily. Things the book's example leaves out that a senior mentions: replication (stored 3 times → ~165 PB), read traffic (Twitter is read-heavy; reads are many times writes), and growth over 5 years.
stages.interaction: A live 'napkin calculator' panel with sliders: MAU (100M–1B), daily % (10–100), tweets/user/day (0.5–10), media % (0–50), media size (100 KB–10 MB), retention years (1–10), replication factor (1–5), peak multiplier (1–10). Outputs update instantly: DAU, write QPS, peak QPS, media/day, total storage. Default = book values (outputs ~3,500 / ~7,000 / 30 TB / ~55 PB). Three challenges (shown as a checklist): (1) 'Make total storage ~165 PB without changing users' → replication 3; (2) 'Double QPS by moving only one slider' → daily % to 100 or tweets/day to 4; (3) 'Find a slider that changes peak QPS but not storage' → peak multiplier. A 'reset to book' button restores defaults.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'The interviewer says: store 3 copies of every file. Your 5-year number becomes…' options: 'About 165 PB' (correct) / 'Still about 55 PB; copies are free' / 'About 55 TB'.

stages.title: Boss: The What-If Wyvern
stages.sub: How does the answer move?
stages.teaches: Applies sensitivity: each assumption scales the result linearly, and some don't touch it at all.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with shared choices: '×2', '×10', '÷2', 'No change'. Each scenario names one change from the book's baseline and asks about one specific output. (1) 'DAU doubles. Write QPS?' → ×2; (2) 'Media share goes from 10% to 20%. Daily media storage?' → ×2; (3) 'Users post 1 tweet a day instead of 2. Peak QPS?' → ÷2; (4) 'Tweet text grows from 140 to 280 characters. Daily media storage?' → No change; (5) 'Peak multiplier goes from 2× to 4×. 5-year storage?' → No change; (6) 'MAU grows from 300 million to 3 billion, same daily %. Daily media storage?' → ×10; (7) 'Retention goes from 5 to 10 years. Total media storage?' → ×2. Each 'why' shows the formula with the changed factor highlighted.
stages.check: Boss HP; first-run hearts at stake.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: The full Twitter estimate in 60 seconds
stages.teaches: Recall of the whole worked example.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'Walk me through estimating Twitter's QPS and storage.' Model answer: 'Assumptions first: 300 million MAU, half use it daily, 2 tweets per user per day, 10% have media at about 1 MB, keep data 5 years. DAU is 150 million, so 300 million tweets a day. Divide by 86,400 seconds: about 3,500 tweets per second, and I'll plan for a 2× peak, about 7,000. Storage is dominated by media: 150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB is 30 TB a day; times 365 times 5 is about 55 PB. Text is only ~60 GB a day, so I ignore it. With 3× replication it's ~165 PB, and reads will be much higher than writes, so next I'd estimate read QPS and a cache.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Stated assumptions first', 'Got ~3,500 QPS and ~7,000 peak', 'Got 30 TB/day and ~55 PB over 5 years', 'Mentioned something the book leaves out (replication, reads, or growth)'.

caveats: The book says its numbers are for the exercise only, not Twitter's real figures.
The 2× peak rule is a simplification. Real spikes can be far larger: Twitter's 2013 record was 143,199 tweets per second against an average of about 5,700, roughly 25×.
The book's 64-byte tweet_id is generous: Twitter's Snowflake IDs are 64 bits (8 bytes). It doesn't matter because media dominates.
Text limit is 280 characters since 2017, and UTF-8 text can use up to 4 bytes per character; still tiny next to media.
The example estimates writes and media only; it ignores replication, read traffic (timelines are read far more than written), metadata/indexes, and user growth over five years.

quests.d: Mock interview: estimate a Twitter-like service end to end, then survive the follow-ups
quests.goal: Your win today: given 'estimate the scale of a Twitter-like service', you can ask for the right assumptions, lay out the estimation plan, compute write/read QPS, storage, cache and server counts with units, handle 'what if' follow-ups, and say what the numbers mean for the design.
quests.bookSections: Whole chapter: powers of two, latency numbers, availability numbers, the Twitter example and every tip (rounding, assumptions, units, commonly asked estimates), framed with the 4-step interview framework from Chapter 3

stages.title: Scope it
stages.sub: Step 1 · ask for the numbers you need (2–3 min)
stages.teaches: Estimation starts like any design question: clarify before computing. Useful questions: How many monthly users? What share is active daily? Posts per user per day? What share have media, and how big? How long do we keep data? How many timeline reads per user per day? What peak factor? Weak questions at this point: 'Which database?' (too early), 'What language?' (doesn't change scale). Write every answer on the assumptions board (book tip). Real-interview note: estimation is usually a few minutes inside a larger design question, and some interviewers skip it; a mock interview isolates it for practice.
stages.interaction: Same interview UI as lesson 0008: a sticky interview clock (budget 10 minutes for the whole gauntlet; each stage advances the clock by a fixed amount, turning amber if the learner overspends via wrong answers or hints), an interviewer chat, and a question deck. Interviewer opens: 'Let's do some napkin math. Estimate the scale of a Twitter-like service.' The learner picks questions from a deck of 9 cards (6 useful, 3 weak). Each useful pick makes the interviewer answer in chat and pins a sticky note: 300 million MAU; 50% daily; 2 posts/user/day; 10% with media, ~1 MB average; keep 5 years; each daily user loads their timeline 10 times a day. Weak picks get a polite redirect ('Let's hold that until we know the scale') and cost 15 seconds on the clock. The stage finishes once all 6 notes are pinned. The board stays visible (collapsible) for the rest of the quest.
stages.check: Q.quiz lock-in: 'Before any math, what's the single most important habit?' options: 'Say your assumptions out loud and write them down' (correct) / 'Compute everything to two decimal places' / 'Pick the database first so the numbers make sense'.

stages.title: Plan the math
stages.sub: Step 2 · lay out what you'll compute, in order
stages.teaches: Book tip: commonly asked estimates are QPS, peak QPS, storage, cache, number of servers. A clean order, so each number feeds the next: DAU → write QPS → peak write QPS → read QPS (and peak) → storage per day → storage over retention (× replication) → cache size → number of servers. Saying the plan first gets interviewer buy-in, mirroring Step 2 of the 4-step framework, and shows structure.
stages.interaction: Tap-in-order: 8 shuffled step chips (DAU, write QPS, peak write QPS, read QPS, storage/day, 5-year storage, cache size, server count). Learner taps them in a sensible order; each tap draws an arrow on a little dependency graph showing which earlier number it uses. Accept any order that respects dependencies (e.g. read QPS may come before or after storage, but DAU must come first, peak after its average, 5-year after per-day, servers after peak QPS). A wrong tap shakes and shows the missing input ('Server count needs peak QPS first'). Then the interviewer says 'Good plan, go.'
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Which estimate needs peak QPS as an input?' options: 'Number of servers' (correct) / 'Daily media storage' / 'DAU'.

stages.title: Crunch it
stages.sub: Step 3 · numbers on the board, with units
stages.teaches: Worked answers (tolerances matter more than exact values): DAU = 150 million. Write QPS = 300 million posts ÷ 86,400 ≈ 3,500; peak ≈ 7,000. Read QPS = 150 million × 10 timeline loads = 1.5 billion/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 17,000 (exact 17,361); peak ≈ 35,000. Read:write ≈ 5:1 by requests (much higher by tweets served, since each timeline load returns many tweets). Media/day = 150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB = 30 TB; 5 years ≈ 55 PB; × 3 replicas ≈ 165 PB. Cache: keep the last day's tweet text + metadata hot: 300 million × ~200 bytes ≈ 60 GB, which fits in memory on a couple of cache nodes (media goes to a CDN, not this cache). Servers: interviewer states one stateless app server handles ~1,000 requests/s at peak, so (7,000 + 35,000) ÷ 1,000 ≈ 42 → ~50 with headroom. Bonus: incoming media bandwidth ≈ 30 TB ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 350 MB/s.
stages.interaction: A whiteboard with 8 rows matching the stage-2 plan; each row has a number input and a unit dropdown (none, /s, GB, TB, PB, servers). The learner fills them in order; the sticky assumption board is beside it. Grading per row: within ±30% of the model = full marks (green); within 3× = 'right order of magnitude' partial (amber, half XP) with the worked line shown; worse = red, worked line shown, clock loses 20 s. Missing unit = amber with a 'label your units' nudge, even if the number is right. Over-precise entries (more than 3 significant figures) trigger a 'round it' chip, no penalty. A 'hint' button per row reveals the formula only, at a 15 s clock cost. When the server-count row is reached, the interviewer drops the assumption '~1,000 requests/s per app server' into the chat.
stages.check: Q.quiz after the board: 'Sanity check: ~3,500 writes/s × 86,400 s ≈ ?' options: 'About 300 million a day, matching our assumption' (correct) / 'About 3 billion a day' / 'About 30 million a day'.

stages.title: Boss: the follow-up barrage
stages.sub: Step 3 · 'what if…?' (latency, nines, and changing numbers)
stages.teaches: Interviewers poke the estimate to see if you can reuse it. This round pulls in latency numbers (2.2) and availability numbers (2.3) as well as the sensitivity rules (2.4).
stages.interaction: Q.boss with per-scenario choices (engine supports scenario.choices), one interviewer emoji per card. (1) '📸 Media share goes to 20%. 5-year media storage?' → 'About 110 PB' / 'About 55 PB' / 'About 1.1 PB'. (2) '🧬 We store 3 replicas. Total?' → 'About 165 PB' / 'About 55 PB, replicas share disks' / 'About 18 PB'. (3) '⚽ World Cup final. Is 2× peak enough?' → 'No: 2× is a rule of thumb; Twitter once hit ~25× its average (143K tweets/s in 2013), so plan for bursts with queues and autoscaling' (correct) / 'Yes, peaks never exceed 2×' / 'Yes, because storage doesn't change'. (4) '🌍 Our US timeline service calls a profile service in Europe 10 times per request, one by one. Latency?' → 'About 1.5 s from round trips alone: batch, or keep profiles in-region' (correct) / 'About 5 ms, it's just network' / 'About 150 ms total'. (5) '🧠 Timeline cache: memory or disk?' → 'Memory: ~100 ns vs a ~10 ms disk seek, and ~60 GB fits in RAM' (correct) / 'Disk: it's cheaper and almost as fast' / 'Neither: read from the database every time'. (6) '🔗 Feed needs 3 services at 99.9% each. What can we promise?' → 'About 99.7% unless we add redundancy' (correct) / '99.9%' / '99.97%'. (7) '🗄️ Can one database server hold all the media?' → 'No: ~55 PB needs object storage, plus a CDN for delivery' (correct) / 'Yes, with a big enough disk' / 'Yes, if we compress it'. Each 'why' shows the math and cites which quest it came from.
stages.check: Boss HP bar; first-run hearts at stake; clock adds 20 s per wrong answer.

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.sub: Step 4 · what the numbers mean for the design
stages.teaches: An estimate is only useful if it changes a decision. Map each number to a design consequence: ~7,000 peak writes/s → more than one comfortable database primary for long-term growth, so plan to partition (shard) tweets; ~35,000 peak reads/s with a 5:1+ read skew → a cache tier and read replicas; ~60 GB hot set → fits in an in-memory cache; ~55 PB media (165 PB replicated) → blob/object storage plus CDN, never the relational DB; ~350 MB/s media ingest → upload path separate from the tweet-write path; ~50 app servers → stateless tier behind a load balancer. Then: restate assumptions, name the biggest uncertainty (peak factor, media size), and say what you'd measure first. Caveat: single-database write limits vary widely with hardware and schema; say 'a few thousand writes per second per primary' as a rough guide, not a fact.
stages.interaction: Match-up: 6 number chips on the left (7K writes/s, 35K reads/s, 60 GB hot set, 55 PB media, 350 MB/s ingest, ~50 servers) and 6 design-consequence cards on the right (shard the tweet store, cache + read replicas, in-memory cache, object storage + CDN, separate upload path, stateless tier + load balancer). Tap one chip then its card to draw a link; wrong links break apart with a hint. Then a 'closing statement' builder: 4 sentence slots (restate assumptions / headline numbers / biggest uncertainty / what I'd do next), each with 3 candidate sentences; one per slot is strong, the others are too vague or too precise. The interview clock stops and shows final time vs the 10-minute budget.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'The interviewer asks: so what? Best answer?' options: 'Media dominates at ~55 PB, so it lives in object storage behind a CDN; the hot tweet set is ~60 GB, so it fits in cache' (correct) / 'The numbers are approximate, so they don't change the design' / 'We need exactly 42 servers'.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: The 90-second estimate + your scorecard
stages.teaches: Full recall of the gauntlet, including the chapter's tips.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'From the top, estimate the scale of a Twitter-like service and tell me what it means.' Model answer: 'I'll state assumptions: 300 million MAU, half daily, 2 posts a day, 10% with ~1 MB media, 10 timeline loads a day, 5-year retention. That's 150 million DAU and 300 million posts a day, so ~3,500 writes per second, ~7,000 at a 2× peak. Reads are 1.5 billion timeline loads a day, ~17,000 per second, ~35,000 at peak. Media is 30 TB a day, ~55 PB over five years, ~165 PB with three replicas, so it goes in object storage behind a CDN. The last day of tweet text is ~60 GB, which fits in an in-memory cache, and memory beats disk by orders of magnitude. At ~1,000 requests per second per server I need ~50 app servers with headroom. My biggest uncertainty is the peak factor: real events have hit 25×, so I'd add queues and autoscaling.' After the drill, a scorecard (like 0008) summarizes: assumptions asked, plan order, rows within tolerance, units labeled, follow-ups won, final clock; stored under a separate localStorage key 'sdq:v1:<id>-interview' following 0008's pattern.
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Stated assumptions first', 'Gave write and read QPS with peaks', 'Gave storage per day and over 5 years (with replication)', 'Gave cache size and server count', 'Tied at least two numbers to design decisions', 'Labeled units and rounded'.

caveats: The book's chapter is a toolkit, not a 'design X' prompt; this boss stretches its Twitter example into a fuller estimate (reads, cache, servers) that the book lists as common asks but does not compute.

The timeline-loads, per-server capacity (~1,000 requests/s) and ~200-byte cached tweet are interviewer-given assumptions for practice, not facts; real per-server throughput ranges from hundreds to tens of thousands of requests per second depending on the work done.
In real interviews, estimation usually takes a few minutes inside Step 1 or 2 of a larger design, and some interviewers skip it; the 10-minute budget here is for practice.
The 2× peak factor is a simplification; real spikes can be ~25× (Twitter, 2013).
Series availability math assumes independent failures; correlated failures make it worse.

cheatsheetOutline: One page, 'Napkin Math' cheat sheet for World 2. (1) Quest 2.1 The Byte Ladder: Table 2-1 (2^10 ≈ thousand/KB … 2^50 ≈ quadrillion/PB), 1 ASCII char = 1 byte = 8 bits, the add-the-exponents trick with the worked 300M × 1 KB = 300 GB example, drift table (2.4% → 12.6%), tips: round (99987/9.1 → 100,000/10) and label units; 86,400 s/day ≈ 10^5 (1M/day ≈ 12/s). (2) Quest 2.2 Latency: compact Table 2-2 grouped into tiers (ns: L1 0.5, branch 5, L2 7, mutex/memory 100; µs: Zippy 1 KB 10, send 2 KB 20, 1 MB from memory 250, DC round trip 500; ms: disk seek 10, 1 MB from network 10, 1 MB from disk 30, CA→NL→CA 150), the five conclusions, and a 'today' footnote (SSDs, speed-of-light floor ~90 ms). (3) Quest 2.3 Nines: Table 2-3 (day/week/month/year for 99% … 99.9999%), formula (1 − A) × period, 'each nine = ÷10', series = multiply, parallel = 1 − (1 − A)^n with the independence caveat, SLA vs SLO vs SLI and error budget. (4) Quest 2.4 Tweet Math: the 5 assumptions and the chain DAU 150M → 300M tweets/day → ~3,500 QPS → ~7,000 peak; tweet size (id 64 B, text 140 B, media 1 MB); 30 TB/day → ~55 PB/5 yr (~165 PB with 3 replicas); sensitivity rules (linear in each factor; peak doesn't touch storage). (5) BOSS Estimation Gauntlet: the 8-step estimation order (DAU → write QPS → peak → read QPS → storage/day → storage/retention → cache → servers), the gauntlet's worked numbers (17K read QPS / 35K peak, 60 GB cache, ~50 servers, 350 MB/s ingest), the number → design-decision map, and a 60-second script. Footer: key caveats (2010-era latencies, 2× peak is a rule of thumb, book's numbers aren't real Twitter data) and source links.
